speechtext:
1.	Did the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or any other department or agency of the government retain Mr. F. P. Brais, Q.C., to investigate and/or prosecute cases of wrongdoing in connection with the admission of immigrants from Italy or elsewhere?
2.	If so, when was he first retained, and how long did his services continue?
3.	What is the full amount of his daily retainer, and what total has been paid over to him during this period?
4.	What have been the results to date in terms of numbers of (a) prosecutions; (b) convictions; (c) acquittals; (d) discharges from government service, and what were the names and positions of the persons proceeded against or discharged in each case?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
maintopic: CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first >part of this question is that the services of Hon. F. P. Brais, Q.C., were retained by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) for the purpose of counselling in prosecutions in Montreal in connection with the admission of Italian immigrants to Canada.
The answer to the second part is that the services of Mr. Brais were retained in November, 1954, and are still continuing.
The answer to the third part is that the question of payment of accounts is one which is of special interest to the Minister of Justice, and I imagine also to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). It can be mentioned, however, that no account has been submitted as yet by Mr. Brais and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will know how much is payable to Mr. Brais only after his account has been received and taxed in the Department of Justice.
The answer to the fourth part is that Mr. B. A. Corbo and Mr. M. E. Lattoni were charged and the preliminary hearing was held in Montreal over a period of more than 12 days. The hearing will be resumed in September, 1956, and the department has now completed its case at this hearing.
There was some additional information about this matter given to the committee on estimates which will be found in the minutes of proceedings of the committee for last year.

maintopic: CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Does the minister mean to say that Mr. Brais has not rendered any account to the department since 1954?

maintopic: CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION

The Secretary of State has tabled a report in accordance with the custom, which report is effective March 31,
1955.	Before we get into the estimates, I wonder whether the minister would bring us up to date with the report as of March 31, 1956, so that we may have the current position of the department to deal with.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have here the page proofs of the report as of March 31, 1956, but it has not been tabled yet. I cannot possibly give my hon. friend all the information contained in it. It has not been tabled yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Why not postpone study
of the estimates until we have the information we need?
Mr. Pallet!: It is rather difficult to deal with a department without having obtained the particular information in respect to each section of it before we come into the house, the only information we have being based on figures in a report over a year old. In the course of the discussion of the estimates, any statements we make may be predicted on this report that is a year old, and anything that is out of line must have the sympathy of the house in that regard. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
This is not a department where there can be very serious changes in policy. If there is any information additional to what is contained in the report already tabled that my hon. friend would like to obtain, I would be pleased to give it to him. There is not very much except additional statistics, for instance, in the patent division, how many further applications have been filed and dealt with. It follows the form of the other report, and there is not very much to be added to the report this year except statistics. If there are any that my hon. friend would wish to obtain, I should be very pleased to give them to him.
Mr. Pallet!: I wonder whether the minister can tell me how many companies were incorporated in the period ended March 31,
1956.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I can say to my hon. friend that during the fiscal year 1955-56 letters
[Mr. Harris.!

patent were granted incorporating 847 companies under part I and 36 corporations without share capital under part II of the Companies Act.
Mr. Pallet!: The first comment I should like to make is with respect to the matter of company incorporations. For the year ended March 31, 1954, the report indicates there were 840 companies incorporated, for the year ended March 31, 1955 exactly the same number, 840, and this year there are only 847. It seems to me that these figures are out of line with the apparent growth of the country. I think you will find that the number of incorporations under provincial charters has increased considerably each year, and it seems to indicate that there may be something wrong with the policy of the department in regard to the creation of corporations or some fundamental defect that prevents companies from being incorporated under this department.
At the expense of repeating myself, may I say that it is significant that in the last year there has only been an increase of seven companies over the year before in a country that is supposed to be expanding and growing as this country is supposed to be doing. Along the same line, I wonder whether the Secretary of State has adopted any particular policies in this regard. There is one question I should like to ask him. What steps, if any, are taken in his department or are contemplated by the department with respect to companies incorporated under dominion charters to ensure that there can be full participation by Canadians in those companies? Are there any requirements contemplated by the department that will make holdings available to Canadians in any company thus created, or rather is it the case that most of these companies created under his department are wholly owned outside Canada? Are they merely incorporated here with a few nominal Canadian directors, perhaps even a majority of the directors but with the majority of the holdings outside the country?
If that is the case, are any steps being taken by his department to ensure that Canadians will have a full opportunity to participate as shareholders in these companies? A very revealing observation was made in the banking and commerce committee just last week about the nature of the shareholdings in finance companies. It was a most revealing observation in that practically every finance company operating in Canada was shown to be wholly owned or almost wholly owned outside this country. I think there is a responsibility on the

minister's doorstep to take cognizance of this situation and, if he sees fit, to take the necessary steps.
There is another subject I should like to mention that is not exactly related to companies. It has to do with the recognition of Canadians for valuable services to their country in all fields of endeavour. Every country in the world has some method of recognizing contributions to the country through some form or other of honorary award. It is a recognition that does not necessarily involve the expenditure of money but it is a recognition of their service and their value to the country. We have our wartime awards, decorations for bravery and the like.
Now that we hope to encourage development in this country, I think that one way of encouraging it is to take these people who have given of their time, ability and energy and give them some form of recognition. That matter is directly within the minister's department. I leave that suggestion with him for his consideration. It certainly does not involve the expenditure of money but it involves the expenditure of considerable thought on his part. These people are entitled to that recognition. They have served their country well in their particular field and they should have some special recognition. That is the only way, in the long run, in which you are going to get people to expend their energies for service rather than for money, namely to let them know that after a lifetime of devoted duty in their particular field they will be honoured by their country. In these times we hear of shortages of people in certain fields. We hear that industry attracts young graduates from universities so that people are not available in the university teaching field. If these institutions are not able to pay these people the money in direct competition with industry and the like, governments are charged with giving them something which is perhaps much more valuable to them than money and which at the same time will encourage them in the direction of their energies for the benefit of this country.
Another question I should like to direct to the minister has to do with the civil service. I wonder whether the minister would tell us during the course of the consideration of the estimates-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
On that question may I say that there is, of course, a special item that deals with the civil service commission. I would much prefer it if my hon. friend would deal with the matter when that item is called. There is a separate item for the civil service commission. I think it would be preferable if he would wait until that item is called.
Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I shall be very happy to do that, Mr. Chairman. I wonder whether the minister would tell us when the report of the commission on patents and trade marks is going to be available?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Again, there is an item that provides for the payment of $20,000 in connection with the Ilsley commission which is investigating the patent and trade mark legislation. I would prefer it if the question were asked of me when the item is considered. It is the last item of the estimates of the Secretary of State department. It is vote 414. An amount of $20,000 is provided in the estimates for that very purpose. I could possibly also mention to my hon. friend that some time ago-I think it was at the end of April-I gave an indication that the report will probably be completed at the beginning of next spring. I was later informed that in respect of the copyright and industrial design legislation the report might be finished by the spring of 1957. The report on patents should be finished shortly after the one on copyright and industrial designs. The commission has considered the possibility of presenting separate reports. Instead of forcing parliament to wait until the full report is completed, it might be possible that a report will first be supplied on copyright and industrial design and then the final report on patents would be submitted.
Mr. Pallet!: I have one comment to make. As the minister may recall, last year he said that he expected this report in about a year. It looks now as though it may be a year or may not be a year.
Now, the history of this particular section of his department has shown that there is a very real need for a certain revision. We are asked to revote money each year, and I gather that up to the end of 1956 the estimated expenditure will be about $45,000, for a commission that cannot tell the minister when it will report or what its findings will be. It seems to me it is time for the minister to start telling the commission to bring in its findings and get a little action in this regard. If patents and copyrights are important, and if their relationship to the field of industrial development in this country is important, I think the minister should exert his influence to see that this commission does get busy. This is not the first time that this matter has been brought up in the house. It has been brought up over the last number of years. Each year the house has been content with the answer, "Well, we know the difficulty and we are attempting to deal with it; we finally have a commission and the commission has promised us the report will be in within a year."

Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: They said, "We hope".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Yes. I urge, as strongly as I am able, that the minister exert pressure on the commission to report soon.
I have one final point to make before I sit down. In reading the memoirs of a former vice-president of the United States I noticed that he said when he became vice-president he was like a man who went on an adventure and was never heard from again. I think the Secretary of State is in great danger of being put in the same position. A man is made Secretary of State and that is the last he is heard from. I hope the minister will take that to heart. I think one very recent illustration was our July 1 holiday, Dominion day. This is a field in which the Secretary of State should have been concerned. He should have made sure that Canadians across this country knew what Dominion day meant. I think, with the greatest respect, that the full significance of the day was not brought home to them. When we come back next year, if he is still here, I hope the Secretary of State will accept the responsibility for these intangibles, if you will, that are in his department and that is one of them. Then we, in Canada, will know exactly what Dominion day means.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
There are just two matters on which I wish to secure information, and one arises out of the remarks made by the hon. member who just resumed his seat, the recognition of Canadians in a manner in keeping with the democratic traditions. I remember so well some years ago when the Right Hon. Mr. King introduced the measure for the creation of the Canada medal. This was to be a decoration awarded to Canadians, and one that would meet the democratic ideal while at the same time setting apart those Canadians who received it as persons who had made important and significant contributions to Canada. But for some reason or other the Canada medal, like the Canada Council seems to have been conceived and brought into existence by legislation and then placed in moth balls. I should like to ascertain from the minister why it is that Canadians are not receiving this decoration. What is holding it back? What is the nature of the revulsion on the part of the government against recommending Canadians for this decoration? When does the minister expect that the first of those to be honoured with this distinctively Canadian order of merit, if I may use that expression, will receive it; for certainly as yet we have never been able to secure any information on this? I feel it would be a very fine thing for Canada if Canadians could have that decoration. I can think of those in the arts, in literature, in science and in other walks of

life to whom this decoration, while of no monetary value, would be a significant one because of the honour it would bring to them by being singled out for the award.
That is the first thing I should like to hear from the minister. Then, I should like to know something about the Great Seal of Canada. I would like to know from him at what stage the words, "Dominion of Canada" were removed from the seal and in place of the word "Dominion" the designation that now appears on the Great Seal that was recently brought into effect was placed there. My recollection is the designation is now "Queen of Canada". Has there been anything in the nature of an order in council passed to remove the description of this country as the Dominion of Canada? Incidentally, the only knowledge I have of the rather devious means adopted to remove this designation was first through the telephone book and then afterwards in one or two statutes.
It is interesting to note that as one reads the debates at the time of confederation and throughout the years this country was invariably described as the Dominion of Canada without any suggestion of subservience whatsoever in that designation. The Statute of Westminster refers to the various dominions, and it has not been amended in any way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the statute says, "A dominion known as Canada"?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, that is what it says.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Not "a country known as-".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The minister can answer me in a moment. I am going to continue. Throughout the years, by all of Canada's leading parliamentarians, until the year 1945 or 1946, the reference in Hansard to Canada was invariably "The Dominion of Canada". I remember so well when the Prime Minister made his maiden speech in this house in 1941. He referred to this country as the Dominion of Canada, quoting at the same time the description of this country as it appears in the British North America Act. How many submissions were made to Her Majesty before the present Great Seal was decided on? Did any of those submissions include the description "Dominion of Canada"? At what time in our history did the Great Seal cease to have any reference to Canada as the Dominion of Canada?
Those are two matters that I should like the minister to enlighten the house and country on, for I feel that there has been much too much change made in this connection without parliament being given the right to decide the question. There are some ministers of the crown-I think of two in particular-who

whenever they speak in this house refer to this country as the Dominion of Canada. They are colleagues of the minister. I should like the minister to explain this change which has taken place so surreptitiously in recent years. I think possibly he will clarify everything when he advises how many alternatives for the Great Seal were submitted to Her Majesty. I seem to remember that when the Great Seal was brought into being reference was made, either by the minister or by some other minister of the cabinet, to the effect that it represented a final decision on the part of Her Majesty after certain alternative Great Seals had been submitted.
These are but two matters at the moment upon which I think the minister could be of considerable assistance to the thinking of our country if he were to enlarge upon them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the Secretary of State is the official channel through whom suggestions and recommendations by members of this house and others are made to Her Majesty or to her personal representative for her gracious consideration, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to make two suggestions for the consideration of the government and Her Majesty. All hon. members of this house, and indeed I hope all citizens of this Dominion of Canada, are of course aware that Her Majesty is the Queen of Canada and the head of the government. However, the awareness of this fact tends to fade in the minds of the public, and indeed I think possibly in the minds of some members of the house, owing to the fact that most of us are not privileged to see Her Majesty in person, save on very rare occasions, except by means of television, newsreels and so on.
If the suggestion had been made 50 years ago that Her Majesty should take up residence for some part of the year in this country or indeed in other dominions it would have been considered impossible, but because of greatly improved transportation facilities in the world and speed with which one can travel from one part of the world to another, or perhaps it would be better to say from one part of the commonwealth to another, there is no reason that I can see why Her Majesty might not give consideration to spending some time in the Kingdom of Canada or possibly I should say in the Dominion of Canada.
I realize that because of her official duties in the United Kingdom it would be impossible for Her Majesty to do this for any great length of time, and it is also possible that other members of the commonwealth such as our sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand might also request Her Majesty to take up residence there for certain periods of time, but I think it might very well be 67509-359
Supply-Secretary of State suggested, and I hope the government will give consideration to recommending this to Her Majesty, that Her Majesty should come in person to this country and officially open each new parliament every four years and at the same time take up residence here for possibly three, four or five months. I can see no reason why this could not be done.
It would keep alive an awareness in the minds of our people that the keystone of our system of government is the crown. By having Her Majesty here in person for even a brief period of three or four months every four or five years the importance of our constitutional monarchy would be impressed, not only upon the minds of the people of this country but upon the minds of our neighbours to the south. I think this would be a very wise thing to do.
The second matter which I wish to mention and which is related to the first concerns the appointment of Her Majesty's personal representatives. In the near future Her Majesty will no doubt be appointing a personal representative other than the present incumbent and I think this matter might well be considered before any such appointment takes place. I do not think for one moment that it would be advisable, as we have done in the past, to continue to have Her Majesty's representatives appointed exclusively from the United Kingdom. I think we have outgrown that, shall I say, but on the other hand I do not think it would be wise to have Her Majesty appoint a Canadian on every occasion. While it may not be so at the present time the fact is that in the future, and we must look to the future in considering these matters, such a practice might lead to appointments of a purely political nature and that would do little less than to create a lack of respect for this very high office, the highest in the land. I think that is something which should be considered. We have seen in similar circumstances that on occasion criticism has been directed at the other place for just such practices.
What would the alternative be? My suggestion, which I believe is concurred in by other members of this house, is one which I think should be considered and carefully explored. I suggest that there should be an exchange of governors general with other members of the commonwealth. I think most of us, indeed I would hope all of us who are members of this house, will agree that the British commonwealth is a fine institution, is a fine example to other countries in the world and is something that should be preserved. Anything that we can do to help keep closer the ties between members of the commonwealth should be encouraged at all times.

Supply-Secretary of State
There is little doubt in my mind that if we were to exchange governors general with other members of the commonwealth it would bring home to the people of Canada the fact that we are members of this great institution. It would also bring home that fact to the people of other countries in the world. They would thus see that there is some tangible relationship between the members of the commonwealth. How often have members of this house been asked by their friends from the south or from other countries just what is our commonwealth. We are told that we have different parliaments but many people do not know the relationship that really exists. They tell us that we have no common defence system, nor any common foreign policy. The stock answer is, "We have the crown as a common symbol". That is a little difficult for other people to understand sometimes because they fail to realize the relationship between the commonwealth countries. Sometimes other countries get a different and mistaken apprehension of the real bonds of culture and friendship that exist between the members of the commonwealth. I think it would help a great deal to show, both to ourselves at home and to our friends in other countries, that there is a definite link between the members of the commonwealth, if we did have an exchange of governors general.
Of course, if this were the case, any person that Her Majesty chose to appoint as her personal representative in one of the commonwealth countries would be clearly above any question of local politics, which is, of course, something not only to be desired but absolutely necessary with this very high office.
In addition to that, of course, as all members know, at the present time the only members of the commonwealth that have governors general are Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Other members of the commonwealth, such as India, Pakistan and Ceylon, at the present time do not have a personal representative of Her Majesty. But there are other countries which are presently part of the empire and not yet members of the commonwealth that will become members of the commonwealth-countries such as Nigeria, the Gold Coast and at some time in the future, no doubt, the West Indies.
If such an arrangement were made whereby members of the commonwealth exchanged governors general, it would certainly point an example to all countries of the world and show that we in the commonwealth do have respect for equality of race, creed and colour. I hope it might even encourage countries such as India or Pakistan to reconsider coming back into a somewhat closer relationship with the commonwealth than at present.


I realize that this is something that might seem a little strange at first in Canada if we possibly had a governor general of a different colour or even a different religion than ourselves. If the commonwealth is to lead the way in the world-I know it is a trite expression and I hesitate to use it, but it is a good one-towards the future brotherhood of man, and if we are going to live on in peace with each other in the world, we have to accept these things. I think this would show the people in other countries that we in the commonwealth mean it.
That is all I have to say at this time. I hope very sincerely that these matters have been and will continue to be kept under consideration by the government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
For several years now the suggestion has been advanced in this house that we should have as a governor general somebody from another part of the commonwealth. However, there are very obvious difficulties, and these difficulties have been created in no small measure by the government.
Consider what would happen if we had as a governor general somebody from India, Ceylon, Pakistan or Nigeria. However would he get past the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration? It simply cannot be done, because the laws of this country are such that these people would not fit into Canada. They could not assimilate themselves in the slightest way. The climate would affect them adversely, for one thing. Therefore, though we in this party would favour such a project, there would have to be either a change in the ministry or a change in the regulations and laws of this country. From my point of view, what ought to happen is a change in the ministry, and certainly a change in the rules and laws because, as they are now administered, they are at the best an aberration and at the worst complete stupidity.
The difficulty in getting somebody from India, Pakistan, Ceylon or, as the hon. member for Oxford suggests, from Nigeria is obviously too great for the present minister of immigration to contemplate, no matter how much we should like to see a governor general coming from some other part of the commonwealth. I myself am not too addicted to the idea of always having someone from the United Kingdom come here to represent Her Majesty; still less am I addicted to the idea of some Canadian politician, past or possibly present, occupying the same high office. It is one that ought to be outside the bounds of political controversy, and I hope that is remembered in the future.
However, there is a question I should like the minister to answer now at this particular

stage. I wonder whether he can give the committee details of the latest report of the custodian of enemy property.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The report of the custodian, which was tabled a few months ago, does indicate that the work of the office is proceeding rapidly now and that the fund still in the hands of the custodian has now reached a figure of $8,334,430. That is the fund which the office of the custodian has acquired as a result of the seizure of enemy property under the act.
There is also the office administration account, which discloses that there is still in the fund for the office administration account the sum of $4,165,878. I mention these figures because they should indicate quite a substantial reduction in so far as the fund and the vested assets of the custodian are concerned. The figures have been reduced greatly. Although it is difficult to say when they will have disposed of the whole of the assets seized, it is hoped that the work can be completed in a not far distant future.
I might also mention that there has been, as the result of what I have already indicated, a reduction in personnel. The custodian's office, which as of December 31, 1954, had a personnel of 50, has reduced its personnel now to 44. During the year 1955, two members of the custodian's office retired under the Civil Service Superannuation Act; two were transferred to other departments of the civil service; one member resigned; and one died. Furthermore, on November 9, 1955-and that is what I wanted to allude to-11 members were given notice that their services would not be required after December 31, 1955, which does indicate that the operations are proceeding in such a way as to justify the thought that the operations might be completed in the not far distant future.

Can the
minister tell me how many claims are still outstanding and against what ex-enemy countries?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
These claims, as my hon. friend knows, are dealt with by the war claims commission. I might say that the total amount of the claims paid to June 30 of this year is $5,068,000. That figure concerns claims against Germany, Hungary, Italy and Japan. The total amount of the claims outstanding is still $136,700,000, approximately, but the greater proportion of this large amount is for claims resulting from loss of property which alone represent the very large figure of $136,358,144. That does not, of course, answer completely the question asked as to how many claims are left to be 67509-3591
Supply-Secretary of State dealt with, but I will try to get that information. I find I have it now. There are still in process 1,536 claims, 1,501 of which are claims from civilians, and then there are 35 claims for maltreatment from prisoners of war or their representatives. I might also indicate that the total number of claims was 13,982 out of which 4,193 have been disallowed and 8,253 have been paid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question which has already been raised in connection with the commission set up under the Inquiries Act to investigate the Patent Act and the Copyright Act. Can the minister give the committee any information as to the terms of reference of the commission? I should also like to have him give information with respect to whether or not the commission makes any investigation of the actions of companies involved in any misuse or manipulation of the Copyright Act and the Patent Act for the purpose of setting up monopolies in this country. I realize it is well known that through the Department of Justice many prosecutions have taken place under the Combines Investigation Act, but I think most of us are quite concerned about monopolies being formed in this country and the ineffectiveness of the Combines Investigation Act. Can the minister inform the committee how many cases that have been prosecuted by the Department of Justice have involved the manipulation or misuse of the Copyright Act or the Patent Act?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I think this information could only be supplied by my colleague, the Minister of Justice. I am not in a position to say how many prosecutions have been instituted by the Department of Justice under the Combines Investigation Act even if some of them did concern the operations of the patent division, but I will try to obtain the information and see whether I can furnish it to my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Can
the minister give us the terms of reference of the commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I think the terms of reference will cover what my hon. friend has in mind. They do allow the commission to deal with organizations which would pool patents of invention, for instance, in order to organize a combine. I definitely think that the terms of reference are wide enough to cover that, and by just reading the first paragraph of those terms I think my hon. friend will see that they do cover that. The first paragraph reads as follows:
That a commission of inquiry be established under the authority of part I of the Inquiries Act, to inquire as to whether federal legislation relating

Supply-Secretary of State in any way to patents of invention, industrial designs, copyright and trade-marks affords reasonable incentives to invention and research, to the development of literary and artistic talent, to creativeness, and to making available to the Canadian public scientific, technical, literary and artistic creations and their applications, adaptations and uses, in a manner and oh terms adequately safeguarding the paramount public interest, the whole in the light of present day economic conditions, scientific, technical and industrial developments, trade practices and any other relevant factors or circumstances, including practices under or related to the said legislation and any relevant international convention to which Canada is a party; to submit to the governor in council a report on its findings . . .
In other words, I definitely think that what my hon. friend has in mind is fully covered by the terms of reference. If the commission is to inquire whether federal legislation relating in any way to patents of invention affords reasonable incentive to invention and research, to the development of literary and artistic talent, etc., in a manner and on terms adequately safeguarding the paramount public interest, I do think this covers what my hon. friend has in mind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Can
the minister state how many of these cases have been referred by the commission to the Department of Justice for review or investigation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not think the commission has yet referred any of these cases, if they have found them in existence, to the Department of Justice. Whether they have found anything of that kind will be disclosed in their report. In their report they might make recommendations to that effect but until such time as the report has been completed I do not think the commission would do that. They would inquire whether what my hon. friend has in mind exists and then in their report would make recommendations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have to go to a committee right away but before I do I have one last question. Would the minister be good enough to state why there is a reduction of $15,000 in the appropriation for the commission this year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am told that the commission simply informed us that they expect to complete their report by next spring and they do not think that the rest of the work to be done requires as much in the way of expenditure as the preceding work did. In other words, most of the evidence has already been submitted and the rest of the work is of a nature that does not justify the expenditure of more than is being requested.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I take it that this will not be a continuing commission with its work continuing over the years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Oh no, that is not what the terms of reference disclose. They indicate that a report will be submitted which will contain their recommendations. As it says at the end of the reference, they will submit a report of their findings to the governor general in council with any recommendations that may appear advisable for changes in the said legislation. In other words, it is not a continuing commission. It is a commission of inquiry and when the inquiry has been completed it will submit its report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Since the minister is now answering questions, I should like to ask him two. They are in reference to a matter about which I was in touch with him some weeks ago. He will recall that I was inquiring of his department with respect to the registration of a certain pension society. I understand that pension societies and companies can register with the department of the Secretary of State. My particular questions are these. When such a society or company is registered, is it obligatory upon them to file with his department an annual financial statement of their affairs? My second question is this. If an annual statement is filed with his department, is that statement open to public scrutiny?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There is a special act-the Pension Fund Societies Act-which deals with the conditions of incorporation. The only thing I recall at the moment of the conditions mentioned in the act is that they may register with the department of the Secretary of State. I shall be obliged to look into the matter in order to see whether they must file an annual statement and whether or not it is open to the public for examination. I shall have to look into the matter and I will try to give an answer a little later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
All right. I will not take up any more time now but I will say this. In the case of a pension society, I believe that any member or any person contributing to that pension fund should have made available to him the annual statement as filed in the Secretary of State's department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with much interest and attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) about a way of recognizing, through the Secretary of State, acts of

bravery performed by worthy Canadians during the year.
For instance, last fall in the city of Verdun, near Montreal, some children nearly lost their lives in an unfortunate fire. We then learned that they had been saved through the heroic action of a milkman by the name of Chipman. However, during the weeks that followed this rescue, newspapers seemed to question the identity of the rescuer and even wondered whether the rescue had actually been made by the man named Chip-man or by someone else. I understand however that the Secretary of State did not investigate the matter too closely and that just the same the George Medal for bravery was awarded to milkman Chipman. The Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) might be able to let us know what reports were made to his office on that occasion, and where matters now stand with regard to the person named Chipman, of Verdun.
That was the first matter I intended to raise.
In the second place, I thank the hon. member for Peel for bringing up this matter of the recognition of acts of bravery. It is very interesting to note that the Secretary of State grants awards to people for acts of bravery and I congratulate the department. However, I wonder-and I should like to stress that point-whether it would not be possible also to recognize the obvious talent of some people who are active in other fields. Many Canadians, throughout the country, and regardless of language or religion, have, each in his own field, made important contributions and rendered great services to the Canadian nation.
I may perhaps be allowed to insist particularly, this afternoon, on the worthy contribution made to Canadian literature generally and perhaps to French-Canadian literature especially, by an obviously gifted young man, a remarkable author who, by the way, was born and raised in the constituency which I have the honour to represent here. Because of this talent and of the personal qualities so characteristic of the man, he had become prominent not only in French Canada but throughout this country. The merits of Mr. Roger Lemelin, well known writer, have been recognized not only by the city of Quebec from whom he has received, only a short time ago, a certificate of honorary citizenship, but also by France. Flattering tributes have also come to him from the United States. At the present time all Canadians are privileged to appreciate the
Supply-Secretary of State remarkable talents of this young man of whom we are so proud and whose work is carried over the airwaves in both the English and the French languages.
He is the author of that remarkable book called "Au pied de la pente douce" (The Town Below) and of that other one to which I have particular reference and which has already been translated into several languages, ''The Plouffe Family" which is carried every day on Canadian television stations.
Mr. Chairman, I should like at this time to speak on behalf, not only of Canadians of the province of Quebec, but of all Canadians in general, so that the department of the Secretary of State may give recognition to the undeniable value of this fellow citizen, who is a credit to his family and his small Quebec home, as well as to the whole people of Canada.
Roger Lemelin is my fellow citizen and I believe that this well-known, very popular and highly esteemed author's competence and contribution to Canada's cultural development should be given official recognition. That would certainly be looked upon favourably all across the country.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to state my personal opinion on a question raised a few minutes ago by two members of different political affiliations and which has not received unanimous approval. I shall state a third point of view as regards the appointment of the governor general of Canada.
I believe we should be proud that a few years ago Canada which, after all, is an adult and autonomous nation, appointed for the first time a Canadian as governor general of Canada. I would not suggest that we should go out and seek in other countries of the commonwealth for people of unquestioned merit to assume the duties of governor general of our country. Rather do I feel that we should stick to the present procedure and appoint an English-speaking Canadian whose successor would, in turn, be a French-speaking Canadian.
I believe that somebody has already proposed that the next governor general of French language be the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent). I have-no objection and I would even approve the choice immediately if the right hon. Prime Minister decides to tender his resignation as Prime Minister of Canada, and I say this jocularly.
I believe that we should proceed in that connection according to the same principle

Supply-Secretary of State which prevails in the House of Commons. We recognize that there are two official languages in Canada. The fact is asserted in the British North America Act. We recognize that principle in the House of Commons by appointing alternately, for each parliament, a French-speaking Speaker and an Englishspeaking Speaker.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the few remarks I have made today in the house should be taken into consideration and that serious thought be given to the possibility of appointing, when the mandate of His Excellency the Governor General expires, a French-speaking Canadian to that honorary office.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I wished to make this afternoon, perhaps contrary to what I usually do, I did not criticize. I hope that those few remarks will be taken into serious consideration by the hon. the Secretary of State and by the government of which he is a minister.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to put a few questions to the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard).
Last year, in this house, I put on the record some figures taken out of the public accounts about the representation of French-speaking Canadians within the federal civil service. This year, I understand that the hon. Secretary of State who now has jurisdiction over the civil service commission has himself ordered an inquiry such as I urged last year, and I wanted to know whether his department had made that inquiry.
To a question which I put to him a few months ago, he answered that in fact he had ordered such an inquiry and that, after waiting a few weeks-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question? Is he saying at this time that I personally ordered an inquiry along the lines he has indicated, or whether such an inquiry has been ordered by the civil service commission. I would like to keep the record straight. This information was requested by the civil service commission, not by myself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I believe that, in his answer to the house, the hon. Secretary of State said that the inquiry had been ordered by the civil service commission, but that the commission was under his jurisdiction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I understand but the civil
service commission is an altogether inde-

pendent organization of which I am simply the spokesman in the House of Commons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
As spokesman for the civil
service commission, is the hon. Secretary of State now in a position to give us the figures brought about by this inquiry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Did the hon. Secretary of State ask the civil service commission to investigate this matter?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Yes, the investigation took
place, because the minister replied in this house that he had the figures in hand. When giving me those figures, would the Secretary of State tell us, if possible, on what basis that inquiry was made as to the proportion of bilingual civil servants in the different departments, so that we may know what this representation can mean? I would say this. If, in an inquiry on bilingual civil servants, you put together telephone operators, elevator men and engineers, you do not get, of course, a true picture of bilingual representation. I mean that you do not get the true representation in certain executive positions. Did the department, for instance, get any figures as to the number of those who get over $5,000 a year, which might indicate a bilingual representation of ''X"?
Then, could the minister tell us first whether his department has been able to find out, say for the last ten years, what has been the percentage of the progress or of the set-back, as the case may be, experienced by bilingualism in the civil service in general, and secondly by the French-Canadian representation in the civil service?
Here are the figures I arrived at last year on the basis of the public accounts report. By looking up the number of French-speaking employees earning over $5,000 a year, I found out that these employees held 13 per cent of the executive positions. Yet these employees are practically the only bilingual employees in the country. I would like to ask the minister if there has been any progress or otherwise since last year? Can he tell us if his department has taken any steps to promote bilingualism in our Canadian nation and especially in the federal civil service? What has he done personally to encourage such a move? Are there any associations, any movements or any places where, thanks to the government, classes are held for employees who need to be bilingual?
The general feeling prevalent amongst most French-Canadians is that, instead of

something positive being done, the problem is dealt with as it arises. There is another impression abroad too, and that is that the government is content to deal with these problems only when they are acute and that nothing active or positive is being done in order to promote bilingualism. And yet bilingualism provides a bond of goodwill between the two great races which share in the destinies of this fine country of ours.
I would therefore like the minister to tell me what he plans to do in the various departments in order to promote bilingualism. I see that bilingual French-speaking employees ' are paid the same salary as English-speaking employees, who speak only one language. As a matter of fact, here, in this parliament, the same salary is paid bilingual stenographers as is paid unilingual ones. There would seem to be an opportunity here of promoting real national unity in this country.

The other question I asked the minister had to do with the use of the word "Dominion" and its removal from the Great Seal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Did it exist? Does my hon. friend know whether it actually existed on the Great Seal?

I saw the actual Great Seal. The minister can answer when he rises. There has been a movement, Mr. Chairman, in the direction of chiselling away the use of "Dominion". speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish first of all to say that no doubt the gifted way in which the hon. member gave the benefit of his knowledge of these matters will be appreciated, and I have listened to his remarks with great interest.
He asked a question concerning the Canada medal, to which he also made allusion a few minutes ago. During his remarks he marvelled at the preciousness of that decoration which has not been awarded to anyone since it has been created. If I am not mistaken, the Canada medal was established in October, 1943, by order in council P.C. 7964. I am not in a position to say whether or not the



Supply-Secretary of State medal has been minted. I think I heard remarks last year to that effect made by someone in this house, but I have not been able to ascertain whether in fact this medal has been minted by the Royal Canadian Mint. One thing appears to be sure, namely, that no award of this medal was ever made, at least to my knowledge, to anyone. Whether or not the enthusiasm to which my hon. friend referred, which was in the mind of the then prime minister when he created it, was shared by the members of this government I do not know. But the fact remains that no such medal was awarded to anyone to my knowledge.
The hon. member also made reference to the Great Seal of Canada which he says-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Before the minister goes on, will he say who the members of the awards co-ordination committee are and whether they recommended anyone for this medal?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No, I may say immediately no recommendation was made by the awards co-ordination committee for the awarding of the Canada medal. The committee's chairman is my deputy minister and the members of the awards co-ordination committee are representatives from at least two or three departments of the government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Who are they?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There is the under secretary of state as chairman; there is a representative of the governor general; there are three representatives of the Department of National Defence; there is a representative of the Department of Labour and of the Department of Transport; and also a representative of the dominion archivist; but they are not necessarily the same people. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: When did it last sit?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It did sit quite recently, if I am not mistaken, a few weeks ago.

speechtext: How often has it sat altogether?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: A number of times, but I cannot possibly say how often.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: With very negative results, I take it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Not necessarily. I think in quite a few cases quite a few representations and recommendations were made and in most cases they were followed.
The hon. member for Prince Albert also referred to the Great Seal of Canada and mentioned the fact, if I understood him correctly, that the expression "The Dominion of Canada" had disappeared from the Great Seal of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I did not say that. I asked if it had, and if there had been any change?

The inscription on the former ' Great Seal of Canada was as follows, and it was in Latin: "George VI, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, Ireland and the British dominions beyond the seas, King, Defender of the Faith. Georgius VI" and then the initials "D. Gratia Mag.", which I unfortunately cannot translate. It would be magnae-
I am not sure. "Brit."

The English words I quoted were a translation of what I am now trying to read and cannot because I have just the abbreviations. I would have to read what they mean one by one, and unfortunately I cannot translate them at the moment.
It has been said that the Great Seal does not contain the words "Dominion of Canada". The previous seal contained a reference to British dominions beyond the seas. I have a copy of a print taken from that seal. The hon. member also said that there seems to be a growing practice of doing away with the word "dominion". I would refer him to the British North America Act but I realize also that the opinion I hold may not be shared by my hon. friend. Section 3 reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's most honourable privy council, to declare by proclamation that, on and after a day therein appointed, not being more than six months after the passing of this act, the provinces of Canada, of Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick shall form and be one dominion under the name of Canada.
If I remember correctly the Prime Minister said at one time that it should be possible

to designate our country as the Dominion of Canada or as Canada. In my opinion either expression could be used, but whether or not this country should be designated as the Dominion of Canada or as Canada would be left to the appreciation of the person concerned.
The hon. member for Prince Albert inquired as to what alternative submissions had been made to Her Majesty in connection with the Great Seal. Mr. Chairman, I think I should answer some questions asked by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard). I should reply first to the remarks made by the hon. member for Quebec West about the George Medal awarded a few months ago to Mr. Edward Chipman. If I remember rightly, the Canada Gazette announced in December 1955 that such a decoration had been awarded. Moreover, if again my memory serves me well, the award of the George Medal had been recommended following an act of bravery on the part of Mr. Chipman in a fire that occurred in December 1954. Since the question was raised by the hon. member for Quebec West, I take this opportunity to inform the house that a decision has been made in this matter, and that it will be made known in the Canada Gazette of this forthcoming Saturday.
(Text):
Possibly I should continue my remarks in English for the benefit of those who might be interested in this matter and who might not be able to follow exactly what I am saying in French. This medal was awarded in December, 1955 as the result of a recommendation made to Her Majesty. Hon. members will recall that after the medal was awarded certain allegations were made in the press that the act of bravery which had been performed by the recipient of the medal was not of a degree to justify the awarding of the medal. Because of that controversy the recipient of the medal has asked permission to have the award cancelled, and has so informed the chairman of the awards co-ordination committee. I can say now that Her Majesty has graciously agreed to have the award cancelled and the notice will appear in the Canada Gazette of this week reading as follows:
Supply-Secretary of State
The Queen has been graciously pleased at the request of Mr. Edward C. Chipman, Verdun, P.Q., to cancel the award of the George Medal to Mr. Chipman, of which notice was published in the Canada Gazette of December 17, 1955.
I can assure the house that the matter was investigated fully and considered in all its aspects. While controversy in regard to a matter of this kind is of course perfectly legitimate and helpful in my opinion it should not be prolonged because it would tend to discredit this very high decoration. As far as I am concerned I would think the fact that the intended recipient of the medal has asked to have the award cancelled does not necessarily indicate that he did not perform an act of bravery. No doubt because of the controversy and the other circumstances he decided that he ought to ask permission to have the award cancelled. The allegations made in the newspapers at the time were that the act of bravery in which he participated might not have been of a degree which justified the awarding of such a high decoration.
I might mention incidentally that this is not the highest decoration awarded to civilians; the highest is the George Cross. When this matter was being discussed by the newspapers it was said that the decoration that had been awarded was the highest that could be awarded to a civilian.
I do not think anything more need be said, nor would it be helpful. In my opinion it would simply help to discredit this medal which is held in such high esteem by the nations of the commonwealth.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lapointe has referred to the problem of bilingualism-and I am stressing those words "problem of bilingualism"-which is of great concern to him, for which I give him great credit. It is a problem which I myself consider of the highest import. I must say that, since I first entered this Canadian parliament, I have always taken every possible step to have such a bilingual group as would reflect great credit not only on the province of Quebec, but on the French-speaking minority that he and I, as well as several others, represent in this house.
First of all, I would like to say a few words in connection with his remarks about an inquiry that is supposed to have been directed by the civil service commission. I do say "directed by the civil service commission" because this is the information contained in the answer I gave at the time. The civil service commission, which is a definitely

Supply-Secretary of State independent organization, had decided for reasons it had considered necessary, to inquire and attempt to determine what was the position in relation to bilingualism in the province of Quebec as well as in the remainder of the country. Following a request by my hon. friend, I informed him of the answer supplied by the civil service commission, and from which the hon. member probably inferred that most departments had not been able to give an adequate reply. I then pointed out that the answer of the civil service commission, which I was endorsing, indicated that it was difficult to determine the degree of bilingualism among employees of the commission. Some of these with English-sounding names nevertheless speak excellent French and, in some cases, even do not know English. The opposite is also true. Some with French-sounding names do not speak French.
There is also that extremely difficult and arduous matter of analysing the degree of bilingualism of an employee of the civil service commission. It is undoubtedly for that reason that only an inadequate answer can be given on the matter, for it is practically impossible to give an accurate reply.
I remember the comments that were made at the time by some newspapermen who blamed me for endorsing that reply which, according to them, was not satisfactory. I wish to repeat that, in my view, it is extremely difficult to determine the degree of bilingualism of a federal civil servant. I would be very glad for suggestions, not only from my hon. friend but from anyone else in this house, as to how investigators should go about determining which civil servants are genuinely bilingual. In very many cases bilingual candidates occupy a position where they need not be bilingual. On the other hand, there are cases where employees who claim to be bilingual are not so at all. That is why it is very difficult to give exact and adequate information on this matter.
Just as my hon. friend, I am convinced that bilingualism is making notable headway in this country. I agree with him that there is still room for improvement. Some time ago, the hon. member introduced in the house a bill containing certain suggestions. At that time, I opposed the bill as it was drafted but I clearly stated that I approved it in principle. By what means the suggestions made in that bill could be implemented that remains to be seen. Personally, I believe, as my hon. friend, that bilingual employees should receive not a preferential but a different treatment, on

account of that extra qualification, and that they should therefore be given preference over any non-bilingual candidate to a civil service position. Some system might be devised to achieve that end. Following the introduction of my hon. friend's bill,-indeed I had done so before that-I discussed the matter at some length with representatives of the civil service commission and I asked them to suggest as soon as possible some amendments to the civil service regulations so as to do justice to the employees concerned.
As I pointed out a moment ago, the commission is an independent organization, but I really hope to be able to convince it to bring about certain changes along the lines I have indicated.

speechtext: Will the minister allow me a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Of course.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister stated a while ago, in his answer, that it was no easy matter to determine the degree of bilingualism of a civil servant. speechtext:
I think I have answered
that. The linguistic knowledge of the candidate is assessed but it is not the subject of a separate examination. Perhaps there should be an examination to determine in the first place the extent of bilingualism of a candidate but I must point out that this qualification is taken into account and is part of the examination. As soon as I receive those suggestions, I shall make the necessary recommendations to the government and the civil service commission.

I should like to refer again to the custodian of enemy property. I need hardly remind the minister of the disgust and dissatisfaction that we felt in British Columbia when the government moved the Japanese inland and in its panic turned over their properties to be sold at a fraction of their value. The Japanese and the public of British Columbia have never been satisfied that these people got a fair deal. I am satisfied to this day that they got a rotten deal, caused by the panic of the government during the war.
For that reason we have had stories of the wealth these people lost, the property they lost and the businesses they lost. In order to try to get at the facts I would ask the minister to give me four figures if at all possible; that is, first of all, the total amount of claims made by Japanese in British Columbia, the total amount paid on those claims, the amount of the claims refused and the amount of the claims still outstanding. I think if we get those four figures we will have the answer to the dissatisfaction that is still rampant among the people who know the Japanese, live with them and in many cases have dealings with them. I hope the minister can give me those figures.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I shall try to obtain those figures. Some of them would be contained in the report of the royal commission that considered this problem at the time, but I will try to get more precise and definite figures from the custodian's office and inform my hon. friend accordingly.

Supply-Secretary of State
I should like to ask the minister whether this committee has made any report in connection with a structure on parliament hill which I believe, more than anything else, is one of the great traditional buildings on this hill. I refer to the old Supreme Court of Canada building, for it was in that building that some of the great parliamentarians of Canada, including prime ministers, appeared as counsel. I think of Edward Blake-

remarks. As I say, I think of Edward Blake, Sir John Thompson, Sir Robert Borden, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and Louis St. Laurent, all prime ministers of Canada who appeared from time to time and made their distinguished names in that building. I should like to ask the minister whether or not the perpetuation or the preservation of that building, great in history-actually the place where our constitution received its major interpretation-should not be a matter of concern, and whether it should not be maintained as part and parcel of those things worth preserving and deserving to be preserved as part of our history, our tradition, and our past.
Indeed, in so far as the constitution is concerned all our future was made in that building. In that place these five outstanding lawyers, four of whom afterwards became prime ministers of Canada and Edward Blake, the leader of the Liberal party in the 1880's and one of Canada's most outstanding lawyers if not the most outstanding one, made their reputation and shaped Canada's future. Has consideration been given by this committee to the need of preserving this building as one of our great and ancient heritages for the benefit of this and future generations?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is probably appropriate that in this week in which we have celebrated Dominion Day as the 89th birthday of this great nation, we should now be discussing in this house matters of tradition and honour. In that regard I should like to draw the attention of the minister and the members of this house to what to me seems a great oversight.
5658	HOUSE OF
Supply-Secretary of State
Earlier this afternoon members of this house spoke of a Canada Medal. I believe some questions were asked with reference to the Canada Council. But recognition for services rendered and work done in Canada has over the years been accorded to Canadian citizens by the government or other bodies in Great Britain. It is true that these particular honours have been valued very highly. There have been practically uncountable awards of C.B.E.'s, O.B.E.'s and M.B.E.'s, though I hear now that there will be no more of these awarded except to members of the armed forces. One outstanding Canadian is the holder of that great and noble award, the Order of Merit. We have a few who have been made Companions of Honour, and the George Medal has been awarded both to military personnel and civilians.
All these things have added, in their own way, to the character of this nation and its outstanding citizens. Other countries honour their outstanding citizens. I speak now in terms of those who have made names for themselves in the artistic world. While our great neighbour to the south possibly is inclined to reward them in a monetary way -something which is no doubt to their satisfaction-and also with some adulation, which may not be completely to their satisfaction, it seems to me that Canada does nothing for its outstanding sons and daughters. Those who have made names for themselves all too frequently wear foreign decorations, without even the recognition of the United Kingdom and certainly with no recognition from Canada. In fact it would seem the only thing Canada does for its outstanding artists is to feed them to the United States market.
There are a great many persons who come to mind, musicians, painters, sculptors, dramatists, writers and others, and a great many actors and actresses who have made names for themselves not only in the United States but abroad. We have young people who find it impossible to acquire recognition in this country, and certainly impossible to make a living here in their chosen field. They go either to the country to the south or to Europe. Of course, that is for them to decide; but there are great people who stay in Canada, who do wonderful work and pile up for this country great honour and prestige.
One of these great men has just recently been accorded a rare honour. I refer to Dr. Healey Willan, the most famous organist and composer on this continent and one of the greatest in the world. A week or so ago he received from the Archbishop of Canterbury the rare Lambeth degree of doctor of music. He was the only composer not resident


in the United Kingdom who was asked to write a homage anthem for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II. We all, as Canadians, I know rejoice in this recognition of a beloved, outstanding Canadian, but I should like to ask the minister if he does not think it is about time that Canada did something for its distinguished citizens.
I am sure that a few years ago Canadians generally thought when the government of this country refused, on behalf of its distinguished citizens, to accept any titles, something would take the place of that recognition of their services. When it was said that the Canada Medal would be awarded under specific circumstances we all believed it. Now it would seem that either through neglect or design this Canada Medal has faded into the fairy tale realm and there is little or no hope of it being awarded or of anything being suggested to take its place. It fills me with great sorrow, Mr. Chairman, when I see persons of the calibre of the great Dr. Willan, who are not recognized in any respect by their own nation.
I trust that the minister will not treat my remarks lightly but will suggest to his colleague that something be done, and soon, to give suitable recognition of Canadian citizens.

speechtext: I should like to address a few remarks to the minister in his capacity as spokeman for the chief electoral officer.

speechtext: I have one question arising out of the discussion this afternoon. Can the minister inform the house if there is actually in existence an approved design for the Canada Medal and if so where it is?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Do I understand that there is presently no approved design that could be examined by any member of this house, or no copy of the medal that could be seen?

I was pleased to have the minister give the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary the assurance that he will be supplied with information concerning the claims of Canadian citizens of Japanese origin. Quite a number of us regretted the hasty manner in which the assets of these Canadians were seized by the custodian of enemy property. All of us, I am sure, regretted the manner in which those assets were disposed of. As a result of those proceedings many of these Canadians applied for compensation. They applied for redress of their grievances. They claimed they had been very shamefully dealt with, and a goodly number of them received further compensation as a result of a commission that was later set up to investigate these claims.
On the whole the findings of this commission were nothing more nor less than a whitewash of the actions of the custodian of enemy property. However, some of these Canadians did receive awards on their claims. When the minister supplies the information I hope he will also be able to supply us with information as to what action was taken against those Canadians who so shamefully possessed themselves of property belonging to their fellow Canadians. What I have in mind, for example, is that some of this furniture was placed in a large warehouse. The warehouse was broken into, and when it came time to sell the furniture it had all disappeared.
There are actually a number of cases where Canadian citizens obtained property at prices that everyone knew to be away out of line. Were any prosecutions launched against those people who collaborated with one another to
Supply-Secretary of State deprive their fellow Canadian citizens of what they owned? I have in mind even such things as forest holdings. Was any legal action taken against anyone for any of the proceedings in those years?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I shall try to obtain this information, which would possibly be available from the Department of Justice, as to whether any prosecutions were launched. I know the matter was fully investigated by a royal commission at the time, and a number of complaints were made afterwards which were then analysed. I do not think I can add very much to what the report contained at the time, but I shall try to obtain information as to whether any legal action was taken by the Department of Justice and inform my hon. friend.
While I am on my feet X would like to answer a question asked by the hon. member for Macleod. The Pension Fund Societies Act, section 16, reads as follows:
Every society formed under this act shall at all times when thereunto required by the governor in council or by either house of parliament make a full return of their property and of their receipts and expenditure for such period and with such details and other information as the governor in council or either house of parliament requires.
I am informed that none of these societies has yet been required to report according to the provisions of this section.

speechtext: In the first item of the details on page 501 I note that last year there was a confidential messenger at $2,760. This year none is mentioned in the estimates.
