speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the Chipman case. I noticed the minister showed some reluctance to discuss that case. I personally do not take that view. I think we should discuss public business here. If this is not the place to discuss it I do not know where we should discuss it. It would appear to me that whether it was through slackness in the minister's department, or where it was, the Governor General, because I presume he was involved, and certainly Her Majesty were put in an embarrassing position.
The minister has told us the award was cancelled at the request of the potential recipient himself. What was the statement of the potential recipient, a man who perhaps has made history by refusing the Queen's medal? What did he say as to his particular unworthiness, if indeed he admitted that in this

Supply-Secretary of State particular case? In other words, what was his reason for refusing the medal? Was it fear of attendant publicity?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I think the recipient of that award, who has asked permission to have it cancelled, would be. the proper person to indicate why he did that. I suggested before, in dealing with these matters which affect the royal prerogative, I did not think it was in keeping with the high regard in which these decorations are held to speculate as to the reasons which justified the cancellation of the award in this case. All I can say is that the matter was fully investigated and the recipient himself, in order to avoid further controversy, thought it advisable to ask permission to have the award cancelled.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister says the matter was fully investigated. I think this is a case of too little and too late. It seems to me that the time for a thorough investigation into the matter was when the request came from somebody or other that representations should be made to Her Majesty through the Governor General. I would like to know who it was that initiated those proceedings, who it was that recommended to the minister or to his department, for I presume it would go through that channel, that such a request should be made to Her Majesty through His Excellency. On whose recommendation was the whole thing initiated?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I should give any more information on that. Whoever makes a recommendation or a representation for the awarding of a decoration of that nature, we consider that information and the matter itself as confidential. The same thing applies to recommendations made by the awards co-ordination committee which considers these requests. The same thing applies to the nature of the recommendation that is then made by the Governor General as well as by the minister in charge of the department.
I do not think my hon. friend should ask for more information than that. I am speaking in a way which I think would indicate that. I would not deny that there is a responsibility somewhere. I am not going to say what was the recommendation or what was the nature of the investigation. All I can say is that it was fully investigated and the recipient of the award decided that, in view of the controversy that had arisen, he would ask permission to have the award cancelled. This request of his was transmitted through the Governor General to Her Majesty, who acceded to the request.
I would think in all sincerity that it would be better to avoid speculation as to what were


the reasons which justified the action on his part and the recommendation on the part of the awards co-ordination committee. I do not think it would serve a useful purpose. I am not going to say the action was taken lightly, either. I simply followed the request made by the recipient of the medal and transmitted his request through the proper channel.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is the minister satisfied that the medal should have been awarded?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not think I should be called upon to answer that question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Surely there must be some responsibility somewhere, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There was quite a controversy in the press. Allegations were made. I had the matter fully analysed by the awards co-ordination committee, and I took the recommendation and transmitted it as it was, the recommendation being that the request made by Mr. Chipman be acceded to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister is talking about speculation. I deny that there is speculation. I am interested in facts, not speculation. I am elected here as an opposition member, and I think it is my business to look into these things. It is the responsibility of the department in which I am interested.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I take full responsibility for everything done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister does?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not think the minister has fully answered my question in regard to the investigation which took place. When did it take place? Did it take place when the recommendation was made to the department by the minister that the representation should be made to Her Majesty through the Governor General, or did it take place afterward, when there was some doubt as to whether or not the man would accept the award? Surely before the event rather than after the event was the time the department should have made a full and thorough investigation, and not put Her Majesty and His Excellency in the peculiar position of having been requested to make an award and then come along later and say, "Would it please Your Majesty to cancel the award." The thing is ridiculous.

speechtext:
The matter was investigated when the recommendation was first made by the awards co-ordination committee. The recommendation was based on information received from what we considered to be

After that investigation had been made there was a recommendation for the award of the medal. The second investigation and recommendation were made by the awards co-ordination committee for cancellation, and that second recommendation I transmitted through the ordinary channels to Her Majesty.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If the minister is prepared to take full responsibility I suppose that is all we can do about the matter. The minister admits the department was wrong.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The deputy ministers did not know what they were doing; possibly they were not capable of assessing bravery.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: May I ask whether this colossal travesty on the Queen resulted from evidence given under oath? Was evidence taken under oath in support of the application? maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Could the minister give the names of the members of the committee that made this recommendation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have no objection to doing that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This was a serious mistake and it would seem to indicate that there was a slip-up somewhere, a failure on the part of the committee to investigate properly. When the minister is replying would he indicate if there have been other similar incidents?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There have been quite a few cases where cancellations have taken place.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
But I am referring to cancellations because of mistakes in the awards. Were those cancellations of the type
Supply-Secretary of State that occurred in the case of Sir Roger Casement who had received certain decorations, including a knighthood, and then became a convicted traitor? An order in council was passed after his conviction removing from him the honours which His Majesty had conferred during the days when he was an administrator of the government of Great Britain and before he launched on a career which ended in his death on the scaffold for treason. In addition to those cases where there have been cancellations because of treasonable activities on the part of the recipients, have there been cases where due to a lack of investigation in peacetime, decorations have been cancelled? If so, would the minister indicate those in his reply?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I never said that this cancellation was made because there had been a lack of investigation. I simply said that the matter was investigated by the awards co-ordination committee, which acted on what it considered to be trustworthy and reliable information upon which to base its recommendations. Afterward representations were made, an investigation was launched and the committee came to the conclusion that they ought to agree to the request made by the recipient to have the award cancelled.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Who were the members of the committee which made the award and of the committee which recommended the cancellation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The same members.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Who were they?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The undersecretary of state as chairman, and there was a representative of the Governor General, of the Department of National Defence, of the Department of Labour, of the Department of Transport and of the dominion archivist. I do not actually have the names.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister was chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The undersecretary of state.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Surely you can get the names?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I said that I would get the names.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that some hon. members on the other side are trying to make a mountain out of a molehill in dealing with this obvious mistake. The gentleman who received this award from this government through a mistake which has now been rescinded in the only common sense way in which it could be done has also for the same act of alleged heroism received the Louis Pasteur medal and the Quebec

Supply-Secretary of State safety league medal, and has been nominated for the humane society medal. Every one of those agencies which grant those very cherished awards has machinery for checking its awards. It seems to me that this whole publicity simply proves that even if you take reasonable precautions you can make a mistake from time to time, such as happened this week in London when Her Majesty was inveigled into interviewing a fake holder of the Victoria Cross.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the Secretary of State if it is the policy of the awards committee or of the department or of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not to award medals to members of the R.C.M.P. for outstanding bravery in the performance of their duties?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No, I cannot say that there is any such policy. If a request has been made and if a person is entitled to a decoration, surely there would be no objection because he was a member of the R.C.M.P.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I understand that some time ago a request was made by various people and organizations, including some members of this house, that an award be given to Corporal Johnstone of British Columbia who in thwarting a bank hold-up absorbed eight of the bandits' shots and in all likelihood saved the lives of a goodly number of people. Instead of an award being granted to him there was great publicity over the fact that he had received a promotion.
Upon investigation I find that he was not given any award at all and that the promotion he received was something he was in line for in any event. The minister admitted to me that he would have received this promotion within six months. It meant an increase of only $25 in his salary, so all the man received by way of award was $150 or six months at $25 per month. To the people of British Columbia that was an insult to the bravery and devotion to duty displayed by this man. If they were going to give him only $150 they should not have bothered giving him anything. The public might have organized and given some recognition of this man's services in the maintenance of law and order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
What I can say is that the R.C.M.P. officer to whom my hon. friend refers may have been deserving of the decoration if he fell within the application of the cases where this award is made, in other words if he performed an act of heroism in saving or attempting to save a human life. But I was informed that the case was never referred to the awards co-ordination committee.
[Mr. Philpott.l

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: In that case I must put on record that the member for Burnaby-Richmond has been getting some cheap publicity, because he appeared on the scene of the accident almost as soon as the police were there. He went on the air and announced to all and sundry that he would see to it that a recommendation would be made that this man be suitably rewarded by a decoration granted by the government. I think that is one of the cheapest political tactics I have ever seen a Liberal member resort to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Reverting to item 412, last year there was considerable complaint about the issuing of patents. Is there any improvement this year with respect to the backlog? Has it been cleaned up?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I think it may be useful for me to give certain information on that point,


and I am pleased that the hon. member has raised the question. The situation has improved to some extent. Although the backlog of applications has increased to a certain extent this year, this is due to the great increase in the number of applications for patents. As of April 1, 1956, there were pending in the patent office 72,608 cases, an increase of 2,892 over last year. I might say that last year the backlog of cases amounted to 69,716. Applications received this year have reached a figure of 21,048, of which 14,505 applications have been allowed and 3,651 have been abandoned, leaving 2,892 which have been added to the pending cases in the department.
This would look as if the situation has further deteriorated, but it has not, because it is important to note this fact. The waiting period for an application to be examined has been cut down by a considerable margin. As an example, where there were over 15,000 applications which were two and a half years old and not processed in any way on April 1, 1955, there are only 8,575 such applications in the office at the present time. The department expects that by the end of the year it will be possible to reduce the waiting period to two and a half years. I may say that in the United States the delay is longer than that. It is about three and a half years there before the application for a patent is dealt with and a patent awarded or the application rejected.
It may also be of interest to my hon. friend to note this fact. More than 90 per cent of the applications for patents come from non-Canadian applicants. Over 70 per cent come from the United States and quite a proportion from the United Kingdom, France and other countries. About 5 per cent to 6 per cent of these applications originate from Canadian applicants. I mention this fact because it may be of interest to note this point. Since it takes approximately three and a half years to process an application in the United States, applicants are not anxious to have their applications dealt with in Canada before they are dealt with in the United States, and in many cases all they do here is to mark time until the application in the United States has been disposed of.
The result has been an increase in the backlog, which has been quite considerable; but it is not a situation that can be corrected because, as I said before, over 90 per cent of these applications come from hon-Canadian residents. In other words, these applications come from other countries. I am told the situation is the same with respect to the

United Kingdom. An applicant for a Canadian patent will wait until such time as his application in the United Kingdom has been disposed of.
I do not know if I make myself clear, but I want to say that it is not in reality a real backlog of Canadian applications. Ninety per cent of these 72,000 applications are applications made by non-residents, and there is not very much we can do about it. If we were to say that we would try to process them more rapidly, then the applicant, being interested in having his application dealt with only when the corresponding application has been dealt with in the other country, would use every possible procedure to delay it, and as a request or an application for a patent for an invention can be amended as often as one wishes the result is that the delay is something we cannot do very much about. I want to mention this because in spite of this condition we find that this year we have cut down by a considerable amount the period of delay between the time the application is made and the time it is dealt with.
I also want to say that I have taken up this matter with both the civil service commission and treasury board in order to try to obtain assistance, and I did get some assistance. From April to June of this year we expect that we will have added nine new engineers and eight technical officers to the staff, with the result that the situation will again improve. I mention that because it has been very difficult to obtain assistance. The problem is not only one of salary but of a scarcity of engineers, not being able to secure enough engineers.
The civil service commission and treasury board have agreed to accept our recommendation that technical officers be appointed who are now examiners in order to do that job, and these technical officers do not need to be graduate officers. All they have to have is three years of engineering study, or be bachelors of science. Then they are accepted as assistants to patent examiners. For the first time I think we have made real progress in increasing the staff to an extent that will,
I hope, enable the applications to be dealt with more rapidly.
I mention this with the reservation I have made before, namely that the situation is largely due to the fact that the applicants, being also applicants for patents in foreign countries, do not insist on having their applications dealt with in Canada before they are dealt with in the country of origin.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
It is an improvement over last year, the fact that you have increased your staff. That seemed to be the difficulty last
Supply-Secretary of State year. There was also another complaint or request that was made by the commissioner who said that there was insufficient space for him to do his work properly. Has that situation been improved?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, I can say that situation has been improved also. The Queen's printer has vacated space which it is expected the patent division will now use. I do not think the problem of space exists now. This move will take place in about two months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I think the picture could be clearer if the minister at some time could tell us what is the average delay between the filing of the applications and the first reports on cases. It is a fact that after the first report has been filed the case is really out of the hands of the patent office and delays are due mainly to replies to be made by the applicants themselves. Still I would be interested if the minister could give us at some time a picture as to the average delay between the filing of the application and the first report of the examiner, because after that his department has no control over any delay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: With the experience my hon. friend has in these matters I think he knows as well as I do that I cannot give a definite answer to that question. This report varies according to practically each case. The first report is never made in the same manner and at the same time. It depends on each application, which is dealt with on its merits. There is no fixed date at which a first report can be made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not mean that. I mean how long does it take a case to reach an examiner for examination? There must be an average. I am sure the commissioner would know that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I can say this. I have already said that before the report is actually made it takes about two and a half years. It was more than that before. Of course there can be an exchange of information before that. Before the actual final report is made it takes two and a half years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am not talking about the final report. I am talking about the first report. When does the examiner get the case?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I do not know what my hon. friend would call the exchange of correspondence between the agent of the applicant and the department. If one of these letters can be called a report, there are a number of reports made, as my hon. friend well knows, and I know he knows.

Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am trying to be helpful to the minister and I hope he takes this question properly, because I am going to tell him that it does not take so long to get the first report from the examiner. The average is much closer to eight or nine months, when it is up to the attorney to answer the patent office's report. The average attorney, as he just said, may wait from a month to six months to reply or obtain further delay. I am trying to justify the position of the patent office by stating the fact that the examiners now are in a position to answer within eight or nine months after an application is filed, in most classes of subjects.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes, I agree with that. That has cut the margin to two and a half years before the procedure is completed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a problem I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. It relates to the conflict between voting days and days of religious observance. The hon. member for Spadina was personally involved in this problem in the by-election in Spadina for which he was nominated, and he himself would have raised it today had he not been unavoidably absent. However, it affects all hon. members in some degree and it certainly affects my constituents, because I have a number of constituents of the Jewish faith, which is the principal religious faith outside of the Christian faiths.
I think the problem was pointed up by the regrettable-if I may use that word-event in connection with the last by-election when, as I recall it, the election writs were issued for September 26 which turned out to be one of the principal Jewish religious days, namely the day of atonement. In the case of two by-elections I believe a new date was fixed, October 24.
It seems to me that is a matter which could very simply be avoided in the future, and I have two suggestions to make to the minister. We of course successfully avoid having elections on Sunday.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I agree with that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
It is an extension of that principle which might be applied by an amendment to section 21 of the Canada Elections Act to provide that neither a general election nor a by-election may be called or

held on specified holy days regarded as such by the people of the Christian faith or the Jewish faith. I mention only those faiths. It may be that when this matter came to be dealt with some further inquiry might be made to see whether there were others who were entitled to have their religious observances respected. I cannot think of any offhand. Certainly one does not suggest that all days of religious observance should be excluded. However, I think a calendar could easily be prepared and be inserted in the act which would meet the reasonable requirements which were overlooked in the instances I have cited.
Another approach to the question would be that which has been adopted in some of the states of the union. I cite the legislation in California. I have a copy of the 1955 assembly bill No. 1760. The bill provides that one who will be unable to go to his polling place on election day by reason of the fact that the tenets of his religion require his attendance at church or religious services on that day or otherwise prevent him from attending at the polls will be classified as an absent voter as defined in the act, and he is entitled to vote at other polls. There they vote by mail, actually. But making an advance poll available would be a solution. Similar legislation is found in some of the other states such as Michigan and Minnesota.
I daresay the problem has been dealt with in many places in different ways. I rather prefer the idea of a calendar, because the solution of using an advance poll would prevent the people involved from taking part in the normal activities of election day and one would not want to deprive anybody of those pleasures.
I therefore commend this problem to the minister. I know he has been thinking about it. I notice that there is no legislation on the matter this session. However, I think it is worthy of notice, particularly as it has come to our attention notably and I hope he will find a solution along one or other of these lines, or something which is perhaps even better which he may devise.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words while we are discussing this item of the estimates concerning the continuing problem, under our present election act, of the number of Canadian citizens who still find themselves disfranchised on election day. As the minister will recall, earlier this session my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre introduced one proposal which was designed to meet a part of this problem. The minister did not see fit to accept the particular proposal contained in that bill. However, so far as I am concerned even if he had agreed

to the proposal tor a wider application of the principle of advance polls, there would still remain, in at least certain sections of Canada, quite a substantial number of the electorate who would find themselves completely disfranchised through no fault of their own.
I am thinking particularly of those sections of our population who are engaged in some of the primary production industries, fishermen, loggers and people of that kind, who normally work in some of the more isolated parts of the country. Many of them have a place of residence in one place and are normally working in another. I think perhaps I can best illustrate the problem by referring to a specific situation which arises in the coastal areas of British Columbia whenever an election is held during the summer; June, July or August, whenever it may come. Under the provisions of the act enumeration of the electors takes place at a certain time, and for the purposes of the forthcoming election the people who are then enumerated are the voters at a certain polling area. Then under certain circumstances they may suddenly find that this no longer is their place of residence. This happens, for example, when we have a fire season closure of the coastal areas in British Columbia. At such time virtually the whole population of our large logging camps, which may amount to 400 or 500 working people, are forced to leave that place of residence where they were enumerated and return to some larger centre such as Vancouver, thus finding that on election day they have no opportunity whatever of casting their ballots. That situation, of course, also applies to a large percentage of the fishermen on the coast of British Columbia if the election takes place during the fishing season.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time I have raised this problem in the house. It is one, so far as I am concerned, that should be dealt with in some satisfactory way. Actually the only feasible way I have been able to think of for dealing with it would be by the introduction into our election act of the absentee vote. I realize there may be a great many practical difficulties in the way of the introduction of the absentee vote into our federal elections act, particularly if it were to have application across the whole country. However, I do feel it could be written into the act in a form that would apply at least within the boundaries of a given province. Then if any resident of British Columbia found himself on election day in some other constituency in British Columbia, an arrangement could be worked out whereby he would be entitled to go in a polling place in the area
Supply-Secretary of State in which he found himself and cast a ballot for a candidate in the constituency where he had been enumerated.
I believe that would be a practical proposition. I think possibly it could be done in such a way that the principle of the absentee ballot could apply in any province where such a provision was already in the provincial election act, and where people would be accustomed to exercising their ballot in that manner.
I know, and probably the minister does, that we have had that principle in the election act of British Columbia for a good many years. Apart from the rather unhappy period when we had the single transferable vote in our provincial election act, the absentee ballot has functioned satisfactorily so far as I have been able to learn. I bring this matter up because I do feel it is something to which the minister and the chief electoral officer should be giving serious consideration.
The number of people who may be disfranchised can vary materially from election to election. Under certain conditions hundreds or thousands of Canadian citizens in a province like British Columbia could be disfranchised through no fault of their own. If one of the logging camps I have mentioned closes down, it means the living accommodation and the cook houses close down as well. These men, whether or not they have any desire to stay in order to exercise their franchise, are compelled to leave. I feel that is a situation which certainly warrants much more serious consideration than it appears to have received up to the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
There are three points only that I should like to mention to the Secretary of State on the matter of elections. I would leave them with him for his consideration. The first point relates to the hours of polling set out in the election act. I know that the act was before a committee and was not changed, but I think any act should be the subject of study and revision. There was a member of that committee, who has now gone to the other place, who was rather outspoken about any change at all being made.
I suggest to the minister that the polls should not close at six o'clock but at seven o'clock, whether it be standard or daylight saving time. I feel this would give an opportunity to many people to vote who by reason of not being able to get home, particularly in suburban ridings of the city, cannot cast their ballots. I understand that time for voting is provided in the act, but very often that is hard to get. Many of the provinces have adopted a freer advance poll than is provided for in the federal act. Some have gone so

Supply-Secretary of State far as to say that if you are going to leave your riding for any reason you may vote at an advance poll.
I would suggest that serious consideration be given to that. After all, it is a person's right to vote, but he also has the necessity of making a living. You have the right and duty to vote as opposed to the necessity of making a living. A man must make a living, but he may wish to exercise his right to vote. I think the problem would be resolved if some provision could be made for allowing anyone who is out of his riding on election day to vote at an advance poll.
My next suggestion, sir, is this. There are many people who are physically unable to vote on election day. I refer to those who are inmates of hospitals, old people's homes and similar institutions.
This may be an unusual suggestion but I have no doubt it has been made before in this house, that some provision be made for a sort of travelling poll under supervision so that inmates of hospitals-

I want to call attention to what I thought was a discrepancy or an anomalous situation in connection with some of the advertisements of competitions sent out by the civil service commission. I have noted this at different times, but I noted it particularly the other day when I received two of those notices in the same mail. I refer to competition No. 56-745, labour legislation analyst. The initial salary is $3,180, which can go up to $3,780. The qualifications for this particular position are graduation from a university of recognized standing, preferably with specialization in English history or political science. In the same mail I received notice of competition No. 56-378 for a geological lapidary technician. The initial salary is $4,050 and the maximum is $4,500. The qualifications are elementary school education with additional credits for further academic training.
The point I wish to make is that in one instance they were asking for a college graduate who must know something about labour laws and who specialized in English history or political science. The initial salary is $3,180. In the second instance, competition No. 56-378, the initial salary is $4,050. All the qualifications required are an elementary school education.
As I say, it seems to me there is a great discrepancy between the salaries for these two positions. One requires simply an elementary education and the other a college

education. Is there any co-ordination among the different departments in the matter of establishing salaries for these different positions? It does seem to me that a situation like this is very poor encouragement to sending boys and girls to college, when a boy with an elementary education can start in with an initial salary of nearly $1,000 above that of a boy with a college education.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Whether there would be a real co-ordinating agency of some kind in the civil service commission which would deal with these differences in salaries suggested at different times I do not know, but there is a study made of salaries paid by the different departments to different categories of civil servants. I know that is a fact because it often happens that I myself raise the point with the commission as to why this salary is paid to a civil servant in one department and that salary is paid to another in some other department. 1 say
Supply-Secretary of State that there is always careful study given to that by the commission and I am sure also by the treasury board. If my hon. friend would like to send me the copies of the notices I shall be pleased to look into it and see what the answer would be to his question.

speechtext: Question No. 535

maintopic: SHELLFISH
speechtext:
What protection is offered the consumer of shellfish in respect to sanitary quality?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
The sanitary quality of shellfish offered for sale in Canada is safeguarded by the efforts of several agencies.
Among the major responsibilities of the public health engineering division of the Department of National Health and Welfare are:
the certification of approved shellfish producers;
the supervision of processing plants to ensure compliance with acceptable standards; and
the vigilant surveillance of producing areas with respect to sanitary conditions likely to affect the bacteriological quality of the water overlaying the shellfish beds.
The weekly reports on tests made on shellfish from key areas are carefully scrutinized and action is taken to have areas closed if this is warranted. Samples for these tests are collected by the Department of Fisheries and tested by the laboratory of hygiene of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
All these measures form part of a program designed for the protection of the consumer of Canadian shellfish here and in the United States. The Canadian consumer of shellfish imported from the United States is similarly protected by a rigid control program maintained by the producing states and supervised by the United States department of health, education and welfare under an agreement between that department and the Canadian Department of National Health and Welfare covering mutually acceptable control measures.
